entry: Central region of the [[Milky Way]] galaxy, marked by a [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]]. It lies at the barycenter of the Milky Way and at a point on the galaxy's rotational axis. The black hole, [[Sagittarius A*]], has a mass of about 4 million solar masses, and part of it is a very compact radio source near the [[Event horizon|event horizon]]. The region is about 8 kiloparsecs (26,000 ly) from Earth, in the direction of the constellations Sagittarius, Ophiuchus, and Scorpius. Around 10 million stars lie within one [[Parsec|parsec]] of the center, dominated by [[Red giant|red giants]], with massive [[Supergiant|supergiants]] and [[Wolf–Rayet star|Wolf–Rayet stars]] formed about 1 million years ago. Interstellar dust blocks visible, ultraviolet, and soft X-ray observation, so astronomers rely on gamma-ray, hard X-ray, infrared, submillimetre, and radio wavelengths. In 1958 the International Astronomical Union adopted the position of Sagittarius A as the zero point for galactic latitude and longitude.

Small nocturnal [[Primate|primates]] native to [[Sub-Saharan Africa|sub-Saharan Africa]], forming the family Galagidae. Galagos, also called bush babies or nagapies ("night monkeys" in [[Afrikaans]]), are grouped into six genera. According to the African Wildlife Foundation, they are the most successful [[Strepsirrhini|strepsirrhine]] primates in Africa in both variety and abundance. Large eyes give good night vision, and bat-like ears help them track insects in the dark. They catch insects on the ground or in the air, and their diet also includes fruit and tree gums. Strong hind limbs and long tails aid leaping and balance. Adults weigh 70 to 314 grams. Females may bear singles, twins, or triplets, and newborns weigh less than one-half ounce (14 g). After six to eight days, mothers carry the infants in their mouths, and the young are fed for six weeks.

Family of mostly small freshwater [[Fish|fish]] of the Southern Hemisphere, comprising seven genera. Most species live in southern Australia or [[New Zealand]], but some are found in South Africa, southern [[South America]], Lord Howe Island, [[New Caledonia]], and the [[Falkland Islands]]. The common galaxias (*Galaxias maculatus*) is probably the most widely naturally distributed freshwater fish in the Southern Hemisphere. Galaxiids are coolwater species of temperate latitudes, and many live in cold, high-altitude rivers, streams, and lakes. Many have a partly marine life cycle, or are amphidromous: larvae hatch in rivers, drift to the sea, and return to fresh water as juveniles, unlike [[Salmon|salmon]], which return only to breed. Exotic [[Trout|trout]] and other salmonids prey on galaxiids and compete with them for food, and numerous localized extinctions have followed. The earliest definitive fossils are from the [[Miocene]] of New Zealand. It is thought that the Antarctic land bridge between Australia and South America may have influenced galaxiid evolution.

Subfield of [[Cosmology|cosmology]] concerned with how galaxies formed and changed over time. It studies how a nearly uniform early universe became structured, and how the first galaxies formed. Galaxy formation is hypothesized to arise from structure-formation theories, beginning with tiny quantum fluctuations after the [[Big Bang]]. The simplest model in general agreement with observations is the Lambda-CDM model, in which clustering and merging let galaxies accumulate mass and so determine their shape. Galaxies fall into two broad groups: blue, star-forming galaxies resembling spirals, and red, non-star-forming galaxies resembling [[Elliptical galaxy|ellipticals]]. Most giant galaxies contain a [[Supermassive black hole|supermassive black hole]] whose mass is tied to that of the galaxy's bulge. The first stars and protogalaxies appeared about 300 million years after the Big Bang, according to observations by the James Webb Space Telescope. The [[Milky Way]] is projected to collide with the [[Andromeda Galaxy]] in about 4.5 billion years.

Largest known gravitationally bound structures in the universe, formed by aggregations of [[Galaxy|galaxies]]. They make up the densest part of the large-scale structure of the universe. Clusters formed relatively recently, between 10 billion years ago and now, after the smallest structures collapsed first. Groups typically contain no more than 50 galaxies within 1 to 2 megaparsecs, with a mass of about 10¹³ solar masses, and they are the most common galaxy structures. The [[Milky Way]] lies in the [[Local Group]] of more than 54 galaxies. Clusters are larger and contain hot intracluster gas at 10⁷ to 10⁸ K, which emits [[X-ray|X-rays]]. In a typical cluster, galaxies make up about 5% of the mass and hot gas about 10%, with the remainder [[Dark matter|dark matter]]. The Bullet Cluster provides the strongest evidence for dark matter, although some researchers, such as Brownstein and Moffat, use modified gravity to explain cluster masses without it. Clusters are often associated with larger, non-gravitationally bound [[Supercluster|superclusters]].

System for grouping [[Galaxy|galaxies]] by visual appearance, shape, structure, and distribution of light. The best-known scheme is the Hubble sequence, devised by [[Edwin Hubble]] in 1926 and later expanded by Gérard de Vaucouleurs and Allan Sandage. Hubble divided galaxies into elliptical, spiral, and lenticular classes. [[Elliptical galaxy|Elliptical galaxies]] are smooth and featureless, rated by degree of ellipticity and denoted E. [[Spiral galaxy|Spiral galaxies]] have a flattened disk, spiral arms, and a central bulge, and are denoted S; about half also have a bar, denoted SB. Lenticular galaxies (S0) have a bulge and disk but no visible spiral structure and little ongoing star formation. The sequence is often drawn as a tuning fork, and it remains the most commonly used system in research and amateur astronomy. In 2019 citizen scientists working through Galaxy Zoo reported that the relationship between spiral arms and the nucleus may need reassessment. Gérard de Vaucouleurs's 1959 extension added rings and lenses to describe spirals more fully.

Greco-Roman physician, surgeon, and philosopher whose writings shaped medicine from antiquity into the Renaissance. Born in Pergamon (present-day Bergama, Turkey), he traveled widely to study medical theories before settling in Rome, where he became personal physician to several emperors, including [[Marcus Aurelius]] and [[Commodus]]. His anatomy and medicine were principally shaped by the theory of the four humors. His anatomical reports were based mainly on [[Dissection|dissection]] of Barbary apes, and later of [[Pig|pigs]], because human dissection was forbidden in the Roman Empire by his time. His views dominated Western medical science for more than 1,300 years. His theory of the [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]] went unchallenged until c. 1242, when Ibn al-Nafis described pulmonary circulation. [[Andreas Vesalius]] published human dissections in *De humani corporis fabrica* in 1543, and Galen's physiology was adapted to them. Galen considered himself both a physician and a [[Philosophy|philosopher]], as his treatise *That the Best Physician Is Also a Philosopher* shows.

Natural mineral form of [[Lead|lead]] sulfide (PbS), the most important ore of lead. Galena, also called lead glance, is one of the most abundant and widely distributed sulfide minerals. It crystallizes in the cubic system, often as octahedra, and is commonly associated with [[Calcite|calcite]] and [[Fluorite|fluorite]]. Some deposits contain up to 0.5% [[Silver|silver]], a byproduct that in revenue far surpasses the main lead ore. The largest known deposit is the Lead Belt of southeastern Missouri. Pure galena is insoluble in water and almost nontoxic under normal handling, but lead sulfide can be highly toxic if swallowed or inhaled.

Historical region spanning southeastern [[Poland]] and western [[Ukraine]]. Named after the medieval city of Halych, it was long part of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]]. Its eastern part was controlled by the [[Kingdom of Galicia–Volhynia]] until the Kingdom of Poland annexed it in 1352. In the partitions of Poland it became a crown land of the [[Austrian Empire]], the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria. It was fought over by Austria-Hungary and Russia in [[World War I]], and later by Poland and Ukraine. Its nucleus lies in the Lviv, Ternopil, and Ivano-Frankivsk oblasts of western Ukraine.

Autonomous community of northwestern [[Spain]], a historic nationality under Spanish law. It comprises the provinces of A Coruña, Lugo, Ourense, and Pontevedra. It is bordered by [[Portugal]] to the south, [[Asturias]] to the east, the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the west, and the Cantabrian Sea to the north. It had a population of 2,714,741 in 2025 and an area of 29,583.91 sq km. Galicia was incorporated into the [[Roman Empire]] after the Cantabrian Wars in 19 BC. In the Middle Ages its kingdom was often leagued with León and then Castile, while keeping its own laws and culture. A Statute of Autonomy approved in 1936 was frustrated by Franco's coup and dictatorship. The 1981 Statute of Autonomy, in force today, provides self-government. Galician and Castilian are both official, and a 2013 survey reported that 51% of the population spoke Galician most often day to day. Farming and fishing were the economic base until industrialization after the mid-20th century.

Four largest [[Jupiter|moons of Jupiter]], in descending size order: Ganymede, Callisto, Io, and Europa. They are visible with binoculars and were discovered in 1610 by [[Galileo Galilei]] and, independently, Simon Marius. They were the first objects found to orbit a planet other than Earth. Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System and surpasses [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] in size, though not in mass. Io, Europa, and Ganymede are in a 4:2:1 orbital resonance. Marius named the moons after mythological figures whom Zeus seduced or abducted, a suggestion of [[Johannes Kepler]]. Their discovery undermined the geocentric Ptolemaic world system.

Small hollow [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]] organ where bile is stored and concentrated before release into the small intestine. Bile is produced by the [[Liver|liver]] and reaches the gallbladder through the common hepatic duct. It is released through the common bile duct into the duodenum, where it aids the [[Digestion|digestion]] of [[Fat|fats]]. In humans the pear-shaped organ lies beneath the liver and holds about 50 mL when fully distended. Gallstones, formed mainly of cholesterol or bilirubin, can cause significant upper-right abdominal pain and are often treated by removing the gallbladder, a cholecystectomy. Inflammation, or cholecystitis, may result from gallstone impaction, infection, or autoimmune disease.

Type of [[Ship|ship]] optimized for propulsion by oars, used in the Mediterranean for warfare, trade, and [[Piracy|piracy]]. Galleys had long, slender hulls, shallow drafts, and low freeboard, and most also carried sails for favorable winds. The type developed in the Mediterranean during antiquity and survived in various forms until the early 19th century. The primary warships of the [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]], Greek, and Roman navies were galleys, and the type remained dominant until the start of the [[Early modern period|early modern period]]. Oars let galleys make progress where sailing ships were becalmed, and their large crews could defend against pirates, which made them among the safest passenger vessels for Christian pilgrims in the High and Late [[Middle Ages]]. Ancient galleys had 15 to 30 pairs of oars. Weapons included rams and catapults, then [[Greek fire]] in the Early Middle Ages and [[Cannon|cannons]] from the 15th century. Full-rigged ships with broadside armament eventually made galleys obsolete.

Roman campaigns against the peoples of [[Gaul]], 58–50 BC. Led by [[Julius Caesar|Gaius Julius Caesar]], the wars were fought against Gallic, Germanic, and Brittonic tribes in present-day France, Belgium, and Switzerland, and extended to Britain and Germania. They began with the migration of the Helvetii in 58 BC. Caesar undertook expeditions across the [[Rhine]] and the [[English Channel]] in 55 BC and the following year. The Roman victory at the Battle of Alesia in 52 BC, after [[Vercingetorix]] led a revolt, crushed the Gallic coalition. Gaul became a Roman province only in 27 BC. The wars were a key factor in Caesar's victory in the civil war, his rise to dictator, and the end of the [[Roman Republic]] and establishment of the [[Roman Empire]]. Caesar's account, *Commentarii de Bello Gallico*, claims that over a million Gauls were killed and that Roman losses were almost zero; modern historians consider it propaganda prone to exaggeration.

Order of heavy-bodied terrestrial birds, also called gallinaceous birds or landfowl. Its five families are Phasianidae, which includes junglefowls, Old World quails, partridges, pheasants, [[Turkey (bird)|turkeys]], peafowl, and [[Grouse|grouse]]; Odontophoridae, the New World quails; Numididae, the [[Guinea fowl]]; Cracidae, including chachalacas and curassows; and Megapodiidae, the incubator birds such as malleefowl and brushturkeys. Galliforms inhabit every continent except [[Antarctica]] and have adapted to most environments except the innermost deserts and perpetually icy regions. Many are important seed dispersers, and many escape predators by running rather than flying. Males of most species are more colorful than females and perform elaborate courtship displays. The name derives from the type genus Gallus, Latin for "rooster". The red junglefowl was domesticated as the [[Chicken|chicken]], and galliforms are farmed as [[Poultry]] for meat and eggs, while wild species are hunted as gamefowl.

Failed Allied campaign of World War I to seize the Turkish straits. Britain, France, and the Russian Empire fought the [[Ottoman Empire]] on the Gallipoli Peninsula from February 1915 to January 1916. A naval attempt to force the [[Dardanelles]] failed, and an amphibious landing began in April 1915. With approximately 250,000 casualties on each side, the land campaign was abandoned. [[Mustafa Kemal Atatürk]] rose to prominence as a commander there and founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923. In Australia and New Zealand, 25 April, the anniversary of the landings, is Anzac Day, which surpasses [[Remembrance Day]] as the most significant commemoration of veterans.

Chemical element with symbol Ga and atomic number 31, a soft, silvery metal. Discovered by the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran in Paris in 1875, gallium fulfilled a prediction by [[Dmitri Mendeleev]] of an element he called eka-aluminum. It does not occur free in nature, but in trace amounts in [[Zinc]] ores such as sphalerite and in [[Bauxite]]. Its melting point, 29.7646 °C, is used as a temperature reference point, and it melts in a person's hands. Gallium alloys with low melting points serve as a non-toxic alternative to [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] in thermometers. Most gallium is used in electronics. Gallium arsenide is used in [[Microwave|microwave]] and [[Infrared|infrared]] circuits, and gallium nitride produces blue and violet [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diodes]] and diode lasers. Gallium has no known natural role in biology, though gallium(III) has been used in some medical applications.

Unit of volume in [[Imperial units|British imperial]] and [[United States customary units|United States customary]] systems. The imperial gallon is defined as 4.54609 [[Litre|liters]] and is or was used in the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, South Africa, and some Caribbean countries. The US gallon is defined as exactly 231 cubic inches, or 3.785411784 L. Both gallons contain four quarts, but their pints differ: an imperial pint has 20 imperial fluid ounces, and a US pint has 16 US fluid ounces. Until 1976 the imperial gallon was defined as the volume of 10 pounds of water at 62 °F. The imperial gallon remains the standard petrol unit in several British Overseas Territories and Caribbean countries, while the United Arab Emirates and Myanmar switched to liters. The [[European Union]] removed the gallon from its primary units in 1994, though the UK and Ireland may still use it as a supplementary unit. The IEEE symbol for both gallons is *gal*, not to be confused with the CGS unit of acceleration, also called the gal.

Mathematical connection between [[Field (mathematics)|field theory]] and [[Group theory|group theory]]. [[Évariste Galois]] introduced it to study the roots of [[Polynomial|polynomials]], characterizing the equations solvable by radicals in terms of the [[Permutation|permutation]] group of their roots. An equation is solvable by radicals if its roots can be written using only integers, [[Nth root|nth roots]], and the four basic arithmetic operations. This generalizes the Abel–Ruffini theorem, which asserts that a general polynomial of degree at least five cannot be solved by radicals. The fundamental theorem of Galois theory reduces certain problems in field theory to group theory, which makes them simpler. The theory shows that doubling the cube and trisecting the angle cannot be done as originally stated, and it is needed to prove the complete list of constructible regular polygons. Galois's work was published by Joseph Liouville fourteen years after his death, and the theory took time to become popular among mathematicians.

City and county town of County Galway, on the River Corrib, in western [[Ireland]]. It is the most populous settlement in Connacht, with 85,910 residents at the 2022 census. The city grew around a fortification completed in 1124 by Tairrdelbach Ua Conchobair, King of Connacht. A charter of 1484 allowed a council and mayoralty. In the [[Middle Ages]] the city was controlled largely by fourteen merchant families, the Tribes of Galway, and it grew into a trading port. Today it is known for the Galway International Arts Festival, and it was European Capital of Culture in 2020 alongside Rijeka in [[Croatia]].

Egyptian army officer and statesman, president of Egypt from 1954 until 1970. He led the Egyptian revolution of 1952 and introduced far-reaching land reforms the following year. After a 1954 assassination attempt by a [[Muslim Brotherhood]] member, he cracked down on the organization and assumed executive office. His nationalization of the [[Suez Canal]] and his victory in the [[Suez Crisis]] made him popular across the Arab world. He formed the United Arab Republic with Syria, which lasted from 1958 to 1961. From 1962 he began major socialist and modernization reforms. Egypt's defeat by Israel in the [[Six-Day War]] of 1967 led him to resign, but popular demonstrations brought him back, and by 1968 he was also prime minister. He launched the War of Attrition to regain the [[Sinai Peninsula|Sinai]]. He died after a heart attack following the [[Arab League]] summit of 1970, and his funeral in [[Cairo]] drew five to six million mourners. Supporters credit him with social justice, Arab unity, and anti-imperialism, while critics cite authoritarianism and human rights violations.

Home [[Video game console|video game console]] developed and marketed by [[Nintendo]]. It was released in Japan on September 14, 2001, and in North America that November. It was Nintendo's fourth major home console, succeeding the [[Nintendo 64]], and it competed with [[PlayStation 2]] and [[Xbox (console)|Microsoft's Xbox]] in the sixth generation. It was the first Nintendo console to use optical discs instead of cartridges, and it was focused on games rather than multimedia. Its controller and exclusive games were praised, but the design was criticized as toy-like. Nintendo sold 21.74 million units worldwide. Production ended in February 2007, after the release of the [[Wii]] in November 2006.

Handheld game console developed and marketed by [[Nintendo]]. Released in Japan on March 21, 2001, and in other regions that June, it succeeded the Game Boy Color with a more powerful 32-bit processor, while remaining backward compatible with earlier Game Boy games. It competed with [[Nokia]]'s N-Gage. The clamshell Game Boy Advance SP followed in 2003, and the Game Boy Micro in 2005. Sales of the series, including revisions, reached 81.51 million units by June 2010. Its successor, the [[Nintendo DS]], launched in November 2004 and was backward compatible with its games.

Handheld game console developed and marketed by [[Nintendo]]. It was released in Japan on April 21, 1989, in North America in July 1989, and in Europe in September 1990. It was Nintendo's first handheld to use ROM cartridges, succeeding the Game & Watch line. Its monochrome display and 8-bit processor reflected priorities of affordability, battery life, and durability over the color graphics of rivals such as Sega's Game Gear. The Game Boy and Game Boy Color together sold an estimated 118.69 million units, and were the bestselling console when discontinued in 2003. The later [[Game Boy Advance]] remained backward compatible with it.

American fantasy drama television series created by David Benioff and D. B. Weiss for [[HBO]]. It adapts the novel series *A Song of Ice and Fire* by [[George R. R. Martin]]. Set in the fictional continents of Westeros and Essos, it ran for eight seasons and 73 episodes, from April 17, 2011, to May 19, 2019. It won 59 Primetime Emmy Awards, the most by a drama series, but its final season drew significant criticism for its reduced length and creative decisions. The prequels *House of the Dragon* and *A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms* premiered in 2022 and 2026.
